title: Cloud Bill Shock
summary: A $3,800-a-month stack serves just 1,200 requests per second. Cut the bill to under $1,000 without breaking anything.
scenario: Your startup's cloud bill just landed: almost $3,800 for a month. The CFO asks one question: how much traffic do we actually serve?

The answer is about 1,200 requests per second. Over time, every incident was "fixed" by adding more of everything: 20 app servers, a gateway cluster, a NoSQL store nobody remembers adding, and six database replicas.
Right-size it. Keep it reliable: no single points of failure, and nothing running above 80% utilization.

objectives.label: Every component at or below 80% utilization

hints: Run the simulation and read the Utilization list. Most components sit below 10%: you are paying for capacity you never use.

Work out what you need. 1,200 rps fits on one app server (1,500 rps), but one is a single point of failure, so two is the floor. Apply the same "two of each" logic everywhere, and delete what doesn't earn its cost.
The API Gateway duplicates the load balancer's job here, and the Legacy Store only adds cost. Try: Load Balancer ×2 → App Server ×2 → Postgres ×2, plus Monitoring. A small cache is optional.
explanation: Capacity planning starts with arithmetic: peak load ÷ per-instance capacity, plus headroom, plus redundancy (N+1). For 1,200 rps on 1,500-rps servers that's 1 + 1 = 2 app servers at about 40% each.

Every extra layer costs money and latency without adding value unless it does a distinct job. A gateway in front of a load balancer only makes sense when you need what it offers: auth, rate limits, API composition.
Over-provisioning hides problems instead of fixing them. Ten times the capacity you need is not resilience; redundancy (no SPOFs) plus sensible headroom (under 70–80%) is.
In real life you'd right-size with autoscaling and load tests, and keep a little more headroom for daily peaks. The principle is the same: measure, then provision for peak plus margin.
